512.title: Rahula awakens
512.hook: the Buddha teaches the six senses as not-self, and Rahula awakens
512.howItsDone: Theravada teachers use this discourse's three questions as a pattern for insight practice: is it permanent, is it unsatisfactory, is it fit to be called self?

segments.voice: Yesterday: punna, full, and Nandaka teaching the nuns until the moon was full. Your line: the moon is full.

A boy taught with a mirror, then a young monk told to be like the earth and like water: Rahula has come up before in this collection. Now, in the hundred and forty-seventh discourse, he's grown. One day near Savatthi, the Buddha reflects that the qualities that ripen into freedom have ripened in Rahula. So after the alms round he says: Rahula, bring your sitting cloth. We'll spend the day in the Dark Forest. A father and a son walk out of the city and sit down under a tree. The text adds that many thousands of gods followed them, wanting to hear.
screen: `THE BOY WITH THE MIRROR, GROWN.` → `BRING YOUR SITTING CLOTH.` → `UNDER A TREE IN THE DARK FOREST.`

segments.voice: The teaching is a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself. Rahula, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what is impermanent, is it suffering or ease? Suffering. And what is impermanent, suffering, bound to change: is it fit to be seen as, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, venerable sir. Then the same three questions for forms, the things the eye sees. For eye-consciousness, the seeing itself. For eye-contact, the meeting of eye and form. For the feeling, perception, choices and awareness that come out of that meeting. Then all of it again, for the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind. The Buddha doesn't announce a doctrine and ask Rahula to accept it. He asks, and lets his son look and say what he sees. The Pali word under every answer is anicca: impermanent, changing. Not only the world out there, but the instrument doing the looking, and the looking itself. Seeing this, the Buddha says, a noble disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with seeing, and becomes dispassionate, and through dispassion the mind is freed. While he was speaking, the text says, Rahula's mind was freed from the taints, through not clinging. And the gods who had followed saw something too: whatever has the nature to arise, all of that has the nature to cease. In the Vinaya's story of his going forth, the boy Rahula asks his father for his inheritance. Here, under a tree, he receives it, as questions.

segments.voice: Eyes open for a moment, notice something you're seeing, and the seeing itself shifting: light, focus, a blink. Then close your eyes: a sound arrives and fades, the chair under you, air on your hands, changing even while you notice. Each time something arises, say quietly, changing, not as a sad word, just as a true one.
Rahula awakens. Anicca, impermanence, seen in the senses themselves: the eye, what it sees, and the seeing. Today's word.
Your line: all of it changing. Said plainly, it can be a calm word, not a sad one. Until tomorrow.

513.title: Six sets of six
513.hook: the eye is not self, forms are not self, seeing is not self
513.howItsDone: The six sense bases are a standard frame for insight meditation in Theravada practice; teachers often walk students through them one at a time, asking whether anything found there is lasting or can be called self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rahula, freed under a tree, seeing that even the eye is changing. Your line: all of it changing.

Thirty-six. That's how many items the hundred and forty-eighth discourse lays out, in six rows of six, like a spreadsheet of experience. It opens in Jeta's Grove at Savatthi with the Buddha announcing a teaching good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end. Then he simply counts. It can sound dry on the page, almost like an inventory. But the text says that while it was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed.
screen: `THIRTY-SIX ITEMS, SIX ROWS OF SIX.` → `JETA'S GROVE, SAVATTHI.` → `SIXTY MONKS FREED.`

segments.voice: Here are the six rows. The six inner bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. The six outer bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and things known by the mind. Six kinds of consciousness, one for each meeting: seeing, hearing, and so on. Six kinds of contact, when sense, object and consciousness come together. Six kinds of feeling born of that contact. Six kinds of craving born of that feeling. Then the argument, and it's short. If anyone says the eye is self, the Buddha says, that doesn't hold. The eye's arising and passing away are plainly seen. If the eye were self, you'd have to say: my self arises and passes away. So the eye is not self. Then he runs the same test down the whole table. Forms: not self. Eye-consciousness: not self. Eye-contact, feeling, craving: not self. Thirty-six times, the same short proof. The Pali word is anatta, not-self. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say nobody is here, or that nothing matters. It says each piece you might point to and call me comes and goes, so it can't be the permanent owner you were looking for. Then the discourse turns practical. When a pleasant feeling comes and you delight in it, a tendency toward lust lies underneath. A painful one, resisted: aversion lies underneath. A neutral one, unnoticed: ignorance. Seeing all six rows clearly, the text says, a person grows disenchanted, and is freed.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let sounds come: a car, your own breath, a hum. Look for the one who owns the hearing: there's the sound, the ear, the hearing, arising and fading; is there anything else, standing apart and permanent? Don't argue with yourself; just look, gently.
Anatta. Not-self: thirty-six pieces of experience, each one arising and passing, so none of them the lasting self, tested row by row. Today's word.
Your line: not self, six times. Thirty-six squares, and the same quiet answer in each. Day five hundred thirteen, done.

514.title: Not inflamed
514.hook: not knowing the eye as it is, one is inflamed; knowing it, one is free
514.howItsDone: Theravada meditators practice sense restraint and bare noticing, seeing what comes through each sense as it actually is; teachers often pair this with calm practice so that, as MN 149 says, calm and insight develop together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anatta, thirty-six pieces of experience, none of them a lasting self. Your line: not self, six times.

A bakery window at the end of a long day. Glazed pastries under warm light, a cake with a perfect swirl. The glass hasn't changed since morning, and the person walking past hadn't wanted cake a minute ago. Now there's heat, a pull, a little restlessness. The hundred and forty-ninth discourse has a word for that state. The Pali is saratta, usually rendered inflamed, or impassioned. And it says the fire doesn't start in the cake or the window. It starts in how things are seen.
screen: `A BAKERY WINDOW, LATE.` → `A SUDDEN PULL.` → `SARATTA: INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the great six sense bases, and it begins with a contrast. When someone doesn't know and see the eye as it actually is, the Buddha says, and doesn't know forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and the feeling that comes from it as they actually are, they become inflamed by lust for all of it. Inflamed, tied up, infatuated, fixed on the sweetness. Then things build. Craving grows. The heaps of clinging pile up for the future. Troubles of body and mind grow, torments grow, fevers grow, and the person feels it, in body and in mind. Now the other side. When someone knows and sees the eye, the forms and the seeing as they actually are, they aren't inflamed. Craving fades. The heaps of clinging shrink. The fevers go down. And this person, the text says, feels ease, in body and in mind. The key phrase is yathabhuta: as it actually is. Not as advertised, not as feared. Notice what's not being blamed. Not the eye. Not the world. The eye is fine. The cake is fine. The problem is the fog between them. Then a surprise. For a person who sees this way, the text says, their view simply is right view, their intention right intention, their effort right effort. The eightfold path comes to fulfillment in them. Calm and insight, it says, run together, evenly yoked. Like two oxen under one yoke, pulling one cart.
screen: `NOT SEEING CLEARLY: INFLAMED` · `CRAVING GROWS, FEVERS GROW` · `SEEING AS IT ACTUALLY IS` · `THE PATH FULFILLS ITSELF` · then, large: `NOT INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on something near you, a sleeve, a table, your knee, and feel just texture and temperature. Notice whether there's a small liking or disliking, a pull toward it or away, and without fixing it, name it: liking, not liking, or neither. Then let the hand go still, and notice the temperature of the mind: warm, cool, still?
Not inflamed. Seeing the senses as they actually are, yathabhuta, so the pull of what's seen doesn't set the mind on fire. Today's word.
Your line: two oxen under one yoke. The cake was never the problem; the fog is what clears. That's day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: Who deserves respect
515.hook: teachers free of greed, hate and delusion deserve respect
515.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities respect for teachers is shown through bowing, offerings and service; the discourses also encourage lay people to watch a teacher's conduct over time, as in MN 150 and MN 47, before placing trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not inflamed, seeing the senses yathabhuta, as they actually are. Your line: two oxen under one yoke.

How do you decide whose advice to trust? Follower counts? A title? A confident voice? In the hundred and fiftieth discourse, the Buddha is walking through Kosala with a large company of monks and stops at a brahmin village called Nagaravinda. The householders come out to meet him. Some bow. Some just exchange polite greetings. Some sit down in silence. And he gives them a question to be ready for, because wanderers from other groups may well ask it.
screen: `WHOSE ADVICE DO YOU TRUST?` → `A BRAHMIN VILLAGE, NAGARAVINDA.` → `A QUESTION TO BE READY FOR.`

segments.voice: Suppose, the Buddha says, wanderers of other groups ask you: which recluses and brahmins should not be honored or respected? Answer like this. Those who aren't free of greed, hate and delusion for what the eye sees, the ear hears, and the rest. Whose minds aren't at peace inside. Who act well one day and badly the next, in body, speech and mind. Why not honor them? Because, the householders would say, we're like that ourselves; we see nothing higher in them. And which should be honored? Those free of greed, hate and delusion toward what the senses bring, whose minds are at peace, who act well steadily, in body, speech and mind. Because we see something higher in them than in ourselves. Notice what's missing. No mention of robes. No mention of which teacher someone follows, or which group. The test makes no exception for the Buddha's own monks. The measure is the same for everyone: what has this person done with greed, hate and delusion? The Pali words are lobha, dosa, moha, the three roots the discourses keep returning to. Then the Buddha supplies the next question those wanderers would ask. How would you know? What's the evidence? The answer is quietly practical. Look at how they live. Such teachers go to the forest, to remote places, where there are no sights or sounds or tastes to delight in. They choose the quiet, and you can see the choice. So respect isn't about rank, and it isn't blind. It's earned by a visible life, and you're allowed to watch before you give it.
screen: `WHICH TEACHERS NOT TO HONOR` · `WHICH TEACHERS TO HONOR` · `THE TEST: GREED, HATE, DELUSION` · `THE EVIDENCE: HOW THEY LIVE` · then, large: `WHO TO RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something without trying to be admired: a grandparent, a coach, a nurse, a friend. Picture how they lived, what they didn't grab, what they didn't hate, what they saw clearly, and let a little gratitude rise. If you like, bow your head slightly, inside or out.
Lobha. Greed, one of the three roots along with dosa and moha: not the title or the group, but the one free of all three, and you can see it in how they live. Today's word.
Your line: who to respect. Confidence is easy to see; a steady, quiet life takes longer. See you tomorrow.

516.title: Reviewing the alms round
516.hook: after the alms walk, ask: did desire arise on the way?
516.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks still walk an alms round, bowl in hand, and looking back over one's actions, taught here and in the earlier advice to Rahula (MN 61), is part of monastic and lay training.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lobha, dosa and moha, the test for who deserves respect. Your line: who to respect.

Sariputta comes out of his solitary sitting one evening in the Bamboo Grove at Rajagaha and goes to the Buddha. Sariputta, the Buddha says, your faculties are clear. Your face is pure and bright. What have you been abiding in? Emptiness, venerable sir. Good, the Buddha says. That is the abiding of great people. And then, instead of praising the meditation further, he talks about something ordinary: the morning walk into town to collect food.
screen: `EVENING, THE BAMBOO GROVE.` → `YOUR FACE IS CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` → `NOW: THE MORNING WALK.`

segments.voice: A monk who wants to dwell in emptiness, the Buddha says, should look back like this. On the road I took into the village for alms, in the place where I walked collecting food, on the road I took back: was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion or aversion in my mind toward the things I saw? The things I heard, smelled, tasted, touched, thought? If he finds there was, he should make an effort to let it go. If there wasn't, he can live with that gladness, training day and night. That's it. A walk, remembered honestly. The alms round, pindapata, is a walk monks still make today in Theravada countries, bowl in hand, receiving whatever is given. So it's a good test: sights of food, smells from kitchens, people kind and people not. Then the discourse widens the review into a long checklist. Have I let go of the five strands of sense pleasure? The five hindrances? Have I understood the five heaps? Developed the foundations of mindfulness, the factors of awakening, the eightfold path? Calm and insight? Each time, the same two answers: if not yet, keep making effort; if so, rest in that gladness. The title means the purification of almsfood: a walk reviewed this way makes the food, and the life it supports, clean. What's striking is the tone. No guilt, no punishment. Just an honest look back at the road, and then the next step. And it's taught to Sariputta, whose bright face the Buddha has just praised. Even he is told to check.
screen: `DID DESIRE ARISE ON THE WAY?` · `IF SO, LET IT GO; IF NOT, BE GLAD` · `THE LONG CHECKLIST` · `A WALK REVIEWED, A LIFE MADE CLEAN` · then, large: `REVIEW THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Replay a recent walk slowly, your trip home, to the store, to the kitchen: the door, the street or hallway, what you saw. Did wanting rise somewhere, or irritation, or a fog, and where was it exactly? If you find something, note it and breathe it out; if you find a stretch that was clear, rest there and be glad.
Pindapata. The alms round: looking back honestly at the road you walked, if desire arose, let it go; if not, be glad and keep training. Today's word.
Your line: review the road. An ordinary walk, looked at honestly, becomes the practice. Day five hundred sixteen.

517.title: Seeing, not swept
517.hook: the last discourse: training the senses is not closing the eyes but seeing without being swept away
517.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators in several schools practice open-eyed awareness and sense restraint in daily life: noticing liking and disliking as they arise and returning to equanimity, rather than avoiding the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pindapata, the alms round, and an honest look back at the road. Your line: review the road.

The last discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings opens with a short, slightly awkward conversation. The Buddha is staying at Kajangala, and a young brahmin named Uttara comes to visit, a student of a teacher called Parasariya. Does your teacher teach the development of the senses? the Buddha asks. Yes, says Uttara. How? Like this: you don't see forms with the eye, and you don't hear sounds with the ear. Then, the Buddha says, a blind person and a deaf person must be very developed indeed.
screen: `THE LAST DISCOURSE.` → `UTTARA'S TEACHER: DON'T SEE.` → `THEN THE BLIND ARE DEVELOPED?`

segments.voice: Uttara goes quiet. The text says he sat silent, shoulders drooping, head down, with nothing to say. The Buddha doesn't press him. He turns to Ananda and teaches the other way, the development of the senses in his own discipline. When someone sees a form with the eye, something agreeable arises, or disagreeable, or both. That's going to happen; eyes see. The trained person understands: this has arisen in me. It's conditioned, it's coarse, it's dependently arisen. But there's something peaceful and fine: equanimity. Then the reaction fades, and equanimity remains. The pictures are about speed. For the eye, as quickly as someone with good sight might open and shut their eyes. For the ear, as quickly as a strong man snaps his fingers. For the nose, like raindrops rolling off a sloping lotus leaf without sticking. For the tongue, like spitting out a bit of saliva gathered on the tip of the tongue. For the body, like a strong man straightening a bent arm. For the mind, like two or three drops of water falling on an iron pan heated all day: they vanish almost at once. The Pali word for the senses here is indriya, the faculties. So the last discourse of the whole collection lands on something modest. Training isn't shutting the senses down. Liking and disliking will still arise. The skill is in what happens next: seeing it, and letting it go before it carries you off. The eyes stay open. You see, and you stay.
screen: `UTTARA, SILENT, SHOULDERS DOWN` · `THIS HAS ARISEN IN ME` · `A BLINK, A SNAP, A DROP ON IRON` · `EYES OPEN, NOT CARRIED OFF` · then, large: `SEE AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze rest, eyes open and soft, on whatever is in front of you, and when a liking or a disliking rises, a little pull or push, notice it: this has arisen. Then let it fall away like water on a hot pan, and come back to just seeing. If a thought drags you off, open and shut your eyes once, and begin again.
Seeing. Not closing the eyes, but seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity before it sweeps you away. Today's word.
Your line: see and stay. The last of the hundred and fifty-two ends with open eyes. Until tomorrow.

518.title: Looking back: the good potter
518.hook: a discourse we passed: the potter Ghatikara, who cared for his blind parents and kept the precepts
518.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching across schools holds up care for parents as a great merit, and lay followers like Ghatikara are remembered as models of a householder's practice: refuge, precepts, honest livelihood and generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seeing, in the last discourse, where liking passes like water on a hot pan. Your line: see and stay.

The Buddha is walking through Kosala with his monks when he stops at a certain spot by the road and smiles. Ananda knows a Buddha doesn't smile without a reason, so he asks. Long ago, the Buddha says, there was a market town right here, and in it lived a potter named Ghatikara. That's the eighty-first discourse, passed by earlier on the way through the collection. It's the story of a man with clay on his hands, and no robe, whom the text holds up as a model.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SMILES BY THE ROAD.` → `A TOWN WAS HERE, LONG AGO.` → `A POTTER NAMED GHATIKARA.`

segments.voice: In the story, Ghatikara lives in the time of an earlier Buddha, Kassapa, and he's that Buddha's chief lay supporter. His best friend is a young brahmin named Jotipala, who doesn't want to go see some shaven-headed recluse. Ghatikara drags him by the belt, and then, astonishingly, by the hair. A potter grabbing a brahmin by the hair! Jotipala decides something serious must be going on, goes, listens, and becomes a monk. The text says that Jotipala was the Buddha himself, long before. So the potter is the friend who got the future Buddha to his first teacher. But the heart of the story is how Ghatikara lives. He keeps the precepts. He's gone for refuge. He won't dig the ground himself, so he makes pots only from clay at broken riverbanks or heaps left by rats. He doesn't haggle: he sets his pots out and tells people to leave some rice or beans and take what they need. And he looks after his parents, who are old and blind. Once, while he's away, Kassapa Buddha comes for alms, finds no one home, and helps himself to rice from the pot. The blind parents are delighted when they hear. Another time Kassapa's hut leaks in the rains, and his monks take the grass from Ghatikara's own roof to fix it. His parents say: take it. The text says his roofless house stayed dry for three months. So a householder, not a monk, is the hero: care for elders, honest trade and steady virtue, done with your hands. And that closes a week: Rahula under the tree, six sets of six, not inflamed, who to respect, review the road, see and stay.
screen: `THE FRIEND DRAGGED BY THE HAIR` · `CLAY FROM BROKEN RIVERBANKS` · `BLIND PARENTS, CARED FOR` · `THE ROOF GIVEN AWAY` · then, large: `THE GOOD POTTER.`
